lessons.title: What Is an Index
lessons.concept: An index is a database structure that improves the speed of data retrieval operations on a table at the cost of additional storage and slower writes (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) because the index must also be maintained. Indexes work like a lookup structure for column values.
lessons.formula: Benefit: faster SELECT/WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY lookups (in many cases). Cost: extra space + write overhead.
lessons.worked_example: If a users table has many rows and queries frequently filter by email, an index on email can help the database locate matching rows faster than scanning the entire table.
mistakes: Assuming indexes always make every query faster
Creating indexes on every column without considering query patterns

lessons.title: Types and Common Usage
lessons.concept: Common index concepts include single-column and composite (multi-column) indexes, and unique indexes that also enforce uniqueness. Indexes are most useful on columns frequently used in WHERE clauses, JOIN conditions, and sometimes ORDER BY/GROUP BY, depending on the query and DBMS.
lessons.formula: Single-column: index(col). Composite: index(col1, col2) (order matters). Unique index: enforces unique values.
lessons.worked_example: A composite index on (last_name, first_name) can help queries filtering by last_name, or by last_name and first_name, but may be less useful for queries filtering only by first_name (depending on DBMS/optimizer).
mistakes: Assuming column order in composite indexes does not matter
Expecting an index to be used regardless of query selectivity or optimizer choice
Confusing unique index with primary key (related but not identical in all contexts)

lessons.title: When Indexes May Not Help
lessons.concept: Indexes may provide little benefit on very small tables, columns with very low selectivity (many repeated values), or when queries read most of the table. Over-indexing can degrade write performance and increase maintenance complexity.
lessons.formula: Consider: table size, selectivity, read/write ratio, query patterns. Measure with execution plans where possible.
lessons.worked_example: Indexing a boolean column like is_active in a table where values are almost evenly split may not significantly speed up queries that return many rows.
mistakes: Indexing low-selectivity columns expecting large gains
Adding indexes without checking actual query workloads
Forgetting that indexes must be updated on data modifications

practice.question: What is the primary purpose of an index in a database table?

options.B: To speed up data retrieval operations
options.D: To prevent all duplicate rows automatically

practice.explanation: Indexes are designed to improve the speed of data retrieval (e.g., SELECT queries with filters/joins), though they add storage and write overhead.

practice.question: Which of the following is a common trade-off of adding indexes?

options.A: Faster reads and faster writes with no extra storage
options.B: Slower reads but no storage cost
options.C: Faster reads but extra storage and slower writes

practice.explanation: Indexes can speed up reads but consume additional storage and require maintenance during INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE operations, which can slow writes.

practice.explanation: A composite (multi-column) index is defined on two or more columns, and the order of columns in the index matters.

options.C: Always containing the same value for all rows

practice.explanation: Columns frequently used for filtering (WHERE), joining (JOIN), or sometimes sorting/grouping are common candidates for indexing.

practice.question: Why might an index on a very low-selectivity column (many repeated values) be less effective?

options.A: Because indexes only work on text
options.B: Because the query may still need to read many rows

practice.explanation: If many rows share the same value, an index lookup may still return a large portion of the table, reducing the performance benefit compared to selective columns.

practice.question: Adding an index generally speeds up reads but can slow down which operations?
practice.explanation: Indexes must be maintained on every data change, so writes become slower and storage increases, in exchange for faster lookups on indexed columns.

practice.question: An index on a database table is most similar in purpose to:

options.A: The index at the back of a book
options.B: A full copy of the table

practice.explanation: Like a book index, a database index maps key values to locations so the engine can find rows quickly without scanning the whole table.

questions.question: Which operation is most likely to become slower after adding many indexes to a table?
questions.explanation: INSERT (and also UPDATE/DELETE) operations may become slower because each relevant index must be updated in addition to the table data.

options.B: Column order can affect how the index is used by queries
options.C: It can only be used if col2 is filtered alone
options.D: It replaces the need for all other indexes

questions.explanation: Composite index column order matters because the index is organized by leading columns; query patterns and optimizer behavior determine effective usage.

questions.question: A unique index on a column primarily helps to:

options.A: Allow duplicate values for faster grouping
options.B: Enforce uniqueness and support lookups on that column
options.D: Store rows in random order only

questions.explanation: A unique index enforces unique values in the indexed column(s) and can also be used by the database to speed up searches on those columns.

questions.question: Which scenario is least likely to benefit from adding an index?

options.A: A large table with frequent searches on a highly selective column
options.B: A small table that is fully scanned quickly
options.C: Frequent JOINs on a key column
options.D: Frequent WHERE filters on a selective column

questions.explanation: On very small tables, a full table scan can already be fast, so the overhead of maintaining and using an index may provide little or no benefit.

questions.question: What should be considered before creating an index?

options.B: Query patterns, read/write ratio, selectivity, and storage/maintenance cost
options.C: Only whether the column is numeric
options.D: Indexes require no maintenance after creation

questions.explanation: Effective indexing depends on how data is queried and modified, how selective the column is, and the costs of extra storage and index maintenance.

questions.question: Which column is typically the best candidate for an index?

options.A: A column rarely used in queries
options.B: A column frequently used in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY
options.C: A column with only one distinct value

questions.explanation: Columns that filter, join, or sort frequently benefit most from indexes; low-cardinality or unused columns give little benefit and add write cost.

questions.question: A plain index on the column name may not be used efficiently by the query optimizer in which case?
questions.explanation: Applying a function like LOWER() to the indexed column transforms the expression; a plain index on name does not match the expression, so an expression index or rewrite would be needed.

options.B: Increased storage and slower write operations

questions.explanation: Each index consumes storage and must be updated on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, so excessive indexes degrade write performance and increase maintenance cost.
